answers.explanation: Topology decides what breaks when a cable fails, how easy the network is to grow, and how much it costs to wire.
They can differ. A network can be cabled as a star while the data is passed around it as a ring.
One dedicated link between exactly two devices is point-to-point.
Without a terminator, the signal reflects off the cable's end and garbles everything else on the bus.
One cable keeps it cheap, but a fault can be anywhere along that cable, and one break takes down the whole bus.
Everyone shares one cable, so only one can talk at a time. A busy bus spends a lot of time recovering from collisions.
Token passing is why rings have no collisions and every device gets a fair, predictable turn.
Rings are collision-free, but each extra device adds delay to every trip around the loop.
That's why standards like FDDI used two rings running in opposite directions.
